solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Guy on time machine with one-off garments!

parts.note: Leo is simply a man's name, any guy

indicators.note: one, the Roman numeral I, is taken off the time machine's name

parts.note: the TARDIS is Doctor Who's time machine

explanation.surface: A man boards a time machine carrying unique items of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one-off' looks like 'unique' but tells you to remove I (one) from TARDIS, leaving TARDS. The exclamation mark nods to the leotard being a one-piece garment.
explanation.definitionFit: Leotards are close-fitting one-piece costumes worn by dancers and gymnasts, so they are items of clothing.

clue.text: Olga's travelling on shallow lake

indicators.note: travelling says the letters move about into a new order

parts.note: the name Olga; the 's stands for is, a link

explanation.surface: A woman called Olga is on a journey across a shallow lake.
explanation.definitionFit: A lagoon is a stretch of shallow water cut off from the sea by a reef or sandbank.

clue.text: Ordinary truth surrounding routine and unwelcome presumptuousness

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for ordinary, as in O level

indicators.note: surrounding says the word for truth goes around the other

parts.note: verity means truth
familiar means routine, well-known

explanation.surface: Plain truth about the daily grind and an unwanted cheekiness.
explanation.walkthrough: O level was the British 'Ordinary level' school exam, hence O for Ordinary.
explanation.definitionFit: Overfamiliarity is treating someone too casually, a presumptuous liberty they did not welcome.

clue.text: The morning belongs to us, love

parts.note: AM, ante meridiem, is the morning
something that belongs to us is ours, our

explanation.surface: A romantic claim that the dawn is ours, darling.
explanation.definitionFit: Amour is French for love, used in English for a love affair.

clue.text: Dress material finally selected by Ms Paige

indicators.note: finally says only the closing letter of selected is wanted

parts.note: Elaine Paige is the British musical theatre singer

explanation.surface: A singer chooses at last what fabric to wear.
explanation.walkthrough: Elaine Paige is a British singer famous for musicals such as Evita.
explanation.definitionFit: Delaine is a light wool or wool-and-cotton fabric used for women's dresses.

clue.text: Dangerous to lose a Liberal judge

indicators.note: to lose says the following letters are dropped from the word meaning dangerous

parts.note: a critical condition is a dangerous one

explanation.surface: It is risky for a Liberal politician to be defeated, a commentator judges.
explanation.definitionFit: A critic is someone who judges and evaluates work such as films or books.

clue.text: Angry about a politician going on the warpath

indicators.note: about says the word for angry goes around the other letters

parts.note: raging means very angry
MP, Member of Parliament, is a politician

explanation.surface: A furious politician sets off on the warpath.
explanation.definitionFit: Rampaging means rushing about violently, behaving aggressively like one on the warpath.

clue.text: Hot tubs also good for making one robust

indicators.note: making says the letters of the first words are made into something new

explanation.surface: Hot tubs are also good for building a person's strength.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for a person who is hardy and resilient, not easily harmed.

clue.text: Maybe London correspondents subject to perverse Sky edict

indicators.note: perverse suggests something twisted, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Reporters in London obey a contrary order from Sky TV.
explanation.walkthrough: The City desk is the British newspaper department covering finance, the City being London's financial district.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's City desk is its team of financial journalists; London's City is one example.

clue.text: Worthy King Edward first to French city

parts.note: GR, Georgius Rex, is King George's royal cipher

indicators.note: first says only the opening letter of Edward is wanted

parts.note: noble means worthy, of high moral character

explanation.surface: A deserving monarch named Edward goes first to visit a city in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King Edward' reads as one monarch (or a potato), but King gives GR and Edward only its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Grenoble is a city in south-eastern France, in the Alps.

clue.text: Could be Sally holding doctor's number

indicators.note: holding says one word contains the other within it

parts.note: Aunt Sally, so Sally could be an aunt
MO, medical officer, is a doctor; the 's is a link meaning has

explanation.surface: A woman perhaps called Sally keeps hold of her doctor's phone number.
explanation.walkthrough: Aunt Sally is a British fairground and pub game of throwing sticks at a dummy, and also a figure set up to be attacked.
explanation.definitionFit: An amount is a quantity or sum, which is a number of things.

clue.text: Competition to find sports equipment, or a masquerade?

parts.note: to spot is to find or notice
a ball is both an item of sports equipment and a dance, such as a masquerade

explanation.surface: A contest in which you locate the gear, or else a fancy-dress party.
explanation.walkthrough: Spot the Ball is a long-running British newspaper contest: guess where the ball was in a photo with it removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Spot the ball is a newspaper prize competition, so it is a contest.

clue.text: What one might suggest to most of the Treasury

indicators.note: most of says only part of the word for treasury is used, one letter being dropped

parts.note: the coffer is the treasury, where funds are kept

explanation.surface: A proposal someone might put to the Treasury department.
explanation.walkthrough: Unusually, 'most of' here drops the first letter rather than the last.
explanation.definitionFit: To offer something is to put it forward, propose or suggest it.

clue.text: Rogue second to get hurt, then arraigned

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous rogue

indicators.note: second says take the second letter of the word get

parts.note: ached means hurt, felt pain

explanation.surface: A villain is hurt a second time, then brought before the court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second to get hurt' reads as a phrase, but 'second' picks the second letter of 'get'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be impeached is to be formally charged with a crime, especially a public official, which is being arraigned.

clue.text: Song opens with slander, say, about Mark

indicators.note: opens says the first letter of song is wanted

parts.note: mud is slander, as in mud-slinging

indicators.note: about says the abbreviation is turned around

parts.note: eg, for example, is what say means

explanation.surface: A song begins with defamation, perhaps concerning someone called Mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A smudge is a smear or blur, a dirty mark.

clue.text: What young Robin calls young Martin?

definitions.text: What young Robin calls young Martin?

parts.words: What young Robin calls young Martin?
parts.note: Robin and Martin are both birds as well as boys' names; a small child's word for any little bird is the childish word given

explanation.surface: A child named Robin calls his little brother Martin by a pet name.
explanation.definitionFit: Dicky bird is nursery talk for a small bird, and a martin is a kind of small bird.

clue.text: Cravings Damien had in back street

indicators.note: had in says the artist is held inside the other letters
back says the abbreviation is read in reverse

parts.note: Damien Hirst is the British artist

explanation.surface: An artist named Damien satisfied his cravings in a back street.
explanation.definitionFit: Thirsts are strong desires or longings, as in a thirst for knowledge.

clue.text: Vocal effect really starts something to make you quiver

parts.note: vibrato is a pulsating effect in singing

indicators.note: starts says the opening letter of really is taken

explanation.surface: A singer's warble truly sets off something that makes you tremble.
explanation.definitionFit: A vibrator is a device that shakes or vibrates, making things tremble.

clue.text: What's permissible to the Italian — isn't!

definitions.text: What's permissible to the Italian — isn't!

parts.note: il is Italian for the
licit means lawful, permissible

explanation.surface: Something allowed to an Italian is forbidden elsewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: LICIT is put to IL; the whole clue then says that something marked this way is not permissible.
explanation.definitionFit: Illicit means forbidden by law or custom, the opposite of allowed.

clue.text: Upmarket transport

indicators.note: up in a down clue says the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: a mart is a market

explanation.surface: A posh, exclusive kind of transport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upmarket' reads as one word meaning posh, but splits into Up, the reversal signal, and market.
explanation.definitionFit: A tram is a streetcar running on rails, a form of public transport.

clue.text: Button had returned with broken leg

indicators.note: returned says the word is read backwards

parts.note: got means had, possessed

indicators.note: broken says the letters of leg are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone with a broken leg came back with a button.
explanation.definitionFit: A toggle is a wooden or plastic bar used as a fastener on a duffel coat, like a button.

clue.text: See 11
Splash out on some Tippex pen dispensers

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Spending money on correction-fluid pen holders.
explanation.definitionFit: To splash out is to spend money freely, so the two are synonyms for paying out.

clue.text: Unoriginal drama eyed suspiciously

indicators.note: suspiciously suggests something shifty, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A derivative play is viewed with suspicion.
explanation.definitionFit: Ready-made ideas are borrowed rather than original, prepared in advance by someone else.

clue.text: Message centre for US state case

parts.note: IN is the postal abbreviation for Indiana
a box is a case or container

explanation.surface: A central office handling messages for an American state's case.
explanation.definitionFit: An inbox is where incoming email or letters collect, the place messages arrive.

clue.text: Former dictator gets award for expression

parts.note: Idi Amin was the former dictator of Uganda
OM, the Order of Merit, is a British award

explanation.surface: An ex-tyrant receives an honour for a turn of phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom is a phrase or way of speaking whose meaning is set by usage.

clue.text: Begins to receive intelligence by way of pub quiz questions?

indicators.note: Begins says the opening letter of each following word is taken

parts.note: via means by way of

explanation.surface: Someone starts to gather knowledge through questions asked in pub quizzes.
explanation.definitionFit: Trivia are unimportant facts, the typical material of pub quiz questions, hence the question mark.

clue.text: I'm so excited to be dressed in new lace underwear!

indicators.note: dressed in says one set of letters is clothed by the other
new says the letters of lace are made into a new arrangement
excited says the letters of I'm so are stirred up

explanation.surface: Someone is thrilled to be wearing new lace lingerie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excited' turns I'M SO into MISO, which is 'dressed in' CALE, from 'new' LACE.
explanation.definitionFit: A camisole is a woman's loose sleeveless undergarment for the upper body.

clue.text: To some extent each day I reflect back on foreign capital

indicators.note: back says the run of letters is read in reverse
to some extent says only part of the following words is used, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: Each day I think back over money from abroad, to a degree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To some extent' takes HDAYIR from 'each day I reflect'; 'back' reverses it. 'reflect back' reads as one phrase but 'reflect' is part of the hidden text.
explanation.definitionFit: Riyadh is the capital city of Saudi Arabia, so a capital abroad.

clue.text: Saw Gilbert & Sullivan adopt weary reporter

indicators.note: adopt says the pair take the other word in, between them

parts.note: G and S is the usual shorthand for the comic opera partnership
limp means weary, lacking energy
ED, editor, stands for a newspaper journalist

explanation.surface: The opera writers take on a tired journalist.
explanation.definitionFit: To glimpse is to catch a brief look at something, so a glimpse is a way of seeing.
